claim: Fast inhibitory neurotransmission in the mammalian nervous system is largely mediated by GABAA receptors.
source: Fast inhibitory neurotransmission in the mammalian nervous system is largely mediated by GABAA receptors, chloride-selective members of the superfamily of pentameric Cys-loop receptors.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive literature, as indicated by the citation (Sigel and Steinmann, 2012) in the Introduction.

claim: GABAA receptors are chloride-selective members of the superfamily of pentameric Cys-loop receptors.
source: Fast inhibitory neurotransmission in the mammalian nervous system is largely mediated by GABAA receptors, chloride-selective members of the superfamily of pentameric Cys-loop receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABAA receptor structure and function, supported by the citation (Sigel and Steinmann, 2012).

claim: Native GABAA receptors are heteromeric assemblies sensitive to many important drugs, from sedatives to anesthetics and anticonvulsant agents.
source: Native GABAA receptors are heteromeric assemblies sensitive to many important drugs, from sedatives to anesthetics and anticonvulsant agents, with mutant forms of GABAA receptors implicated in multiple neurological diseases.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in pharmacology and neuroscience, as well as citations throughout the Introduction (Braat and Kooy, 2015).

claim: Mutant forms of GABAA receptors are implicated in multiple neurological diseases.
source: Native GABAA receptors are heteromeric assemblies sensitive to many important drugs, from sedatives to anesthetics and anticonvulsant agents, with mutant forms of GABAA receptors implicated in multiple neurological diseases.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Introduction linking GABAA receptor mutations to epilepsy syndromes (Hirose, 2014) and other neurological conditions (Rudolph and Möhler, 2014).

claim: The structure of a tri-heteromeric α1β1γ2SEM GABAA receptor in complex with GABA was determined by single particle cryo-EM at 3.1–3.8 Å resolution.
source: Here we present the structure of a tri-heteromeric α1β1γ2SEM GABAA receptor in complex with GABA, determined by single particle cryo-EM at 3.1–3.8 Å resolution, elucidating molecular principles of receptor assembly and agonist binding.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including the cryo-EM reconstruction and resolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Remarkable N-linked glycosylation on the α1 subunit occludes the extracellular vestibule of the ion channel.
source: Remarkable N-linked glycosylation on the α1 subunit occludes the extracellular vestibule of the ion channel and is poised to modulate receptor assembly and perhaps ion channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density maps showing glycosylation at Asn110 of the α1 subunit within the extracellular vestibule, as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: N-linked glycosylation on the α1 subunit is poised to modulate receptor assembly and perhaps ion channel gating.
source: Remarkable N-linked glycosylation on the α1 subunit occludes the extracellular vestibule of the ion channel and is poised to modulate receptor assembly and perhaps ion channel gating.
evidence: This is based on inference from the structural data showing the glycosylation occupies a substantial portion of the ECD vestibule and makes specific contacts with the γ2S subunit, combined with speculation about functional implications.

claim: Mutations in GABAA receptor genes are directly linked to epilepsy syndromes.
source: In accord with their crucial role in brain function, mutations in GABAA receptor genes are directly linked to epilepsy syndromes (Hirose, 2014) and are associated with schizophrenia, autism, alcohol dependence, manic depression and eating disorder syndromes (Rudolph and Möhler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Hirose, 2014) which provides evidence for the link between GABAA receptor mutations and epilepsy.

claim: GABAA receptor mutations are associated with schizophrenia, autism, alcohol dependence, manic depression and eating disorder syndromes.
source: In accord with their crucial role in brain function, mutations in GABAA receptor genes are directly linked to epilepsy syndromes (Hirose, 2014) and are associated with schizophrenia, autism, alcohol dependence, manic depression and eating disorder syndromes (Rudolph and Möhler, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Rudolph and Möhler, 2014) which provides evidence for these associations.

claim: GABAA receptors are the targets of a large number of important therapeutic drugs, from sedatives, sleep aids and anticonvulsant medications to anesthetic agents.
source: Moreover, GABAA receptors are the targets of a large number of important therapeutic drugs, from sedatives, sleep aids and anticonvulsant medications to anesthetic agents (Braat and Kooy, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Braat and Kooy, 2015) and represents established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: GABAA receptors are the target of alcohol and are implicated in alcohol dependence.
source: GABAA receptors are also the target of alcohol and are implicated in alcohol dependence (Trudell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Trudell et al., 2014).

claim: GABAA receptors belong to the pentameric ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC) superfamily.
source: GABAA receptors belong to the pentameric ligand-gated ion channel (pLGIC) superfamily (Thompson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation (Thompson et al., 2010).

claim: Other members of the pLGIC family include nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChR), 5-HT3A, glycine, and the invertebrate GluCl and Zn2+-activated cation channels.
source: Other members of this family are nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChR), 5-HT3A, glycine, and the invertebrate GluCl and Zn2+-activated cation channels (Thompson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation (Thompson et al., 2010).

claim: Members of the pLGIC superfamily are composed of five protein subunits.
source: Members of the pLGIC superfamily are composed of five protein subunits and each subunit contains four transmembrane domains (M1–M4) along with extracellular N- and C- termini.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGIC receptors supported by the citation (Thompson et al., 2010).

claim: Each subunit of pLGIC receptors contains four transmembrane domains (M1–M4) along with extracellular N- and C- termini.
source: Members of the pLGIC superfamily are composed of five protein subunits and each subunit contains four transmembrane domains (M1–M4) along with extracellular N- and C- termini.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about pLGIC receptors supported by the citation (Thompson et al., 2010).

claim: GABAA receptors are typically found as heteromeric channels derived from a pool of 19 possible subunits: α1–6, β1–3, γ1–3, δ, ɛ, θ, π, and ρ1–3.
source: GABAA receptors are typically found as heteromeric channels derived from a pool of 19 possible subunits: α1–6, β1–3, γ1–3, δ, ɛ, θ, π, and ρ1–3 (Sigel and Steinmann, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation (Sigel and Steinmann, 2012).

claim: The most prevalent subunit combination in the vertebrate brain is the tri-heteromeric receptor composed of two α, two β and one γ subunit.
source: The large number of subunits gives rise to many possible pentameric assemblies; nevertheless, the most prevalent subunit combination in the vertebrate brain is the tri-heteromeric receptor composed of two α, two β and one γ subunit (Chang et al., 1996; Farrar et al., 1999; Tretter et al., 1997), with the arrangement of subunits being β-α-β-γ-α, in a clockwise order when viewed from the extracellular space (Baumann et al., 2001; Baumann et al., 2002; Baur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Chang et al., 1996; Farrar et al., 1999; Tretter et al., 1997).

claim: The arrangement of subunits in the tri-heteromeric GABAA receptor is β-α-β-γ-α, in a clockwise order when viewed from the extracellular space.
source: The large number of subunits gives rise to many possible pentameric assemblies; nevertheless, the most prevalent subunit combination in the vertebrate brain is the tri-heteromeric receptor composed of two α, two β and one γ subunit (Chang et al., 1996; Farrar et al., 1999; Tretter et al., 1997), with the arrangement of subunits being β-α-β-γ-α, in a clockwise order when viewed from the extracellular space (Baumann et al., 2001; Baumann et al., 2002; Baur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Baumann et al., 2001; Baumann et al., 2002; Baur et al., 2006) and confirmed by the structural data in this manuscript.

claim: The molecular basis for selective subunit assembly of GABAA receptors is not well understood.
source: The molecular basis for selective subunit assembly of GABAA receptors is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The transmembrane ion channel pore is lined by the M2 helices.
source: These studies, together with a large number of biochemical and biophysical experiments, have defined the transmembrane ion channel pore, its lining by the M2 helices and likely mechanisms of ion selectivity (Cymes and Grosman, 2016; Sine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Cymes and Grosman, 2016; Sine et al., 2010).

claim: The extracellular N-terminal domain harbors the orthosteric agonist binding site, located at subunit interfaces.
source: The extracellular N-terminal domain harbors the orthosteric agonist binding site, located at subunit interfaces, in addition to multiple binding sites for an array of small molecules and ions that act as allosteric modulators (Lynagh and Pless, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the citation (Lynagh and Pless, 2014).

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor binds muscimol with a Kd of 109.3 nM.
source: Kd = 5.49 nM (95% CI = 4.25–7.05 nM) or 109.3 nM (95% CI = 91.76–129.7 nM) for [Methyl-3H]flunitrazepam and [3H]muscimol, respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor binds flunitrazepam with a Kd of 5.49 nM.
source: Kd = 5.49 nM (95% CI = 4.25–7.05 nM) or 109.3 nM (95% CI = 91.76–129.7 nM) for [Methyl-3H]flunitrazepam and [3H]muscimol, respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor exhibits ion channel gating properties that are similar to the wild-type receptor in the presence and in the absence of the 8E3 Fab.
source: Moreover, the α1β1γ2SEM receptor also exhibits ion channel gating properties that are similar to the wild-type receptor in the presence and in the absence of the 8E3 Fab (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and comparison to literature (Li et al., 2013).

claim: The cryo-EM construct retains potentiation by diazepam, but the extent of potentiation is reduced for the Fab complex.
source: We note, however, that while the cryo-EM construct retains potentiation by diazepam, the extent of potentiation is reduced for the Fab complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a-b.

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor has a clockwise subunit arrangement of α1-β1*-γ2S-α1*-β1 when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane.
source: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor hews to the classic architecture of Cys-loop receptors, first established by cryo-EM studies of the nicotinic receptor (Toyoshima and Unwin, 1988; Unwin, 1993; Unwin, 2005), with a clockwise subunit arrangement of α1-β1*-γ2S-α1*-β1 when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and confirmed by the Fab binding pattern, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: The arrangement of subunits in the α1β1γ2SEM receptor is in agreement with previous biochemical studies.
source: The arrangement of subunits in this heteromeric complex, as mapped out by the α1-specific Fab fragments, is in agreement with previous biochemical studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Baur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the structural data with previous biochemical studies (Baur et al., 2006).

claim: The epitope of the 8E3 Fab resides entirely on the periphery of the α1 ECDs.
source: The epitope of the Fab resides entirely on the periphery of the α1 ECDs and the Fab buries approximately 760 Å2 of surface area in the interface with the receptor.
evidence: This is determined from analysis of the cryo-EM structure, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The 8E3 Fab buries approximately 760 Å2 of surface area in the interface with the receptor.
source: The epitope of the Fab resides entirely on the periphery of the α1 ECDs and the Fab buries approximately 760 Å2 of surface area in the interface with the receptor.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure using buried surface area analysis.

claim: Most of the receptor residues that interact with the 8E3 Fab are located on the β8, β9 and β10 elements of secondary structure.
source: Most of the receptor residues that interact with the Fab are located on the β8, β9 and β10 elements of secondary structure (Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: This is determined from analysis of the cryo-EM structure, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: The 8E3 Fab binding site does not overlap with the C-loop and is unlikely to directly influence agonist binding.
source: While the Fab binding site is near the crucial C-loop, we note that it does not overlap with it and thus the Fab is unlikely to directly influence agonist binding, in agreement with the agonist binding experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis combined with experimental binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Within the ECD, each subunit buries as much as 1150–1600 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area within each subunit interface.
source: Here, we estimate that within the ECD each subunit buries as much as 1150–1600 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area within each subunit interface (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure using buried surface area analysis, as reported in Supplementary file 2.

claim: There are five unique subunit interfaces in the tri-heteromeric receptor.
source: There are five unique subunit interfaces in the tri-heteromeric receptor and, while we observed a similar arrangement of the ECDs at each interface, we also found subtle differences due to variations in amino acid sequences and in local protein structure.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are solvent accessible fenestrations at subunit interfaces in the ECD that 'connect' the extracellular solution with the extracellular vestibule.
source: There are solvent accessible fenestrations at subunit interfaces in the ECD that 'connect' the extracellular solution with the extracellular vestibule, possibly providing an alternative pathway for ions to access the ion channel (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 2A, with speculation about functional implications.

claim: At the α(+)/β(-) interface, there is a conserved interaction between Tyr209 at the beginning of β10 from the α subunit at the (+) face to Arg117 at β5 in (–) face.
source: As examples, at the α(+)/β(-) interface (Figure 2B), there is a conserved interaction between Tyr209 at the beginning of β10 from the α subunit at the (+) face to Arg117 at β5 in (–) face, as well as a hydrogen bond between Tyr206 from the α subunit and Gln64 from the β subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At the α(+)/β(-) interface, there is a hydrogen bond between Tyr206 from the α subunit and Gln64 from the β subunit.
source: As examples, at the α(+)/β(-) interface (Figure 2B), there is a conserved interaction between Tyr209 at the beginning of β10 from the α subunit at the (+) face to Arg117 at β5 in (–) face, as well as a hydrogen bond between Tyr206 from the α subunit and Gln64 from the β subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The conformation of the ECD in the α1β1γ2SEM receptor most resembles the conformation of glycine/ivermectin-bound GlyR.
source: Nevertheless, if we compare the pentagon formed by joining a line through the center of mass of these individual ECDs, we observe that these are rotated in comparison to our current structure and that our current structure most resembles the conformation of glycine/ivermectin-bound GlyR.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other pLGIC structures, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conformation of the ECD represents an agonist/allosteric modulator bound, activated-like state.
source: Thus, we propose that the conformation of the ECD represents an agonist/allosteric modulator bound, activated-like state.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison with other structures and the presence of GABA in the structure.

claim: There are three substantive densities within the neurotransmitter binding sites, at the interface between the β*(+)/α(-), the α(+)/β(-) and the β(+)/α*(-) subunits.
source: There are three substantive densities within the neurotransmitter binding sites, at the interface between the β*(+)/α(-), the α(+)/β(-) and the β(+)/α*(-) subunits, an observation that diverges from previous studies suggesting that there are only two canonical GABA binding sites located at the β*(+)/α(-) and β(+)/α*(-) interfaces (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Chua and Chebib, 2017).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps as shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observation of three GABA binding sites diverges from previous studies suggesting that there are only two canonical GABA binding sites located at the β*(+)/α(-) and β(+)/α*(-) interfaces.
source: There are three substantive densities within the neurotransmitter binding sites, at the interface between the β*(+)/α(-), the α(+)/β(-) and the β(+)/α*(-) subunits, an observation that diverges from previous studies suggesting that there are only two canonical GABA binding sites located at the β*(+)/α(-) and β(+)/α*(-) interfaces (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Chua and Chebib, 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structural data with previous literature (Chua and Chebib, 2017).

claim: The density feature at the β(+)/α*(-) interface is weaker than that at the β*(+)/α(-) site.
source: The oval-like densities in the two canonical sites are well fit by the chemical structure of GABA, although the density feature at the β(+)/α*(-) interface is weaker than that at the β*(+)/α(-) site (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The third density feature at the α(+)/β(-) interface has the strongest density.
source: Interestingly, the third feature at the α(+)/β(-) interface, with a sausage-like shape, has the strongest density (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the canonical binding sites, the amino group of GABA likely forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Tyr157, Glu155 and Tyr 97.
source: The amino group of GABA likely forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Tyr157 (loop B), Glu155 (loop B) and Tyr 97 (loop A) and a cation-π interaction with Tyr205, while the carboxylate group forms possible hydrogen bonds with Thr129 (β6 strand) and Thr202 (loop C) and a salt bridge with Arg66 (β2 strand).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model of GABA bound to the receptor, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amino group of GABA forms a cation-π interaction with Tyr205.
source: The amino group of GABA likely forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Tyr157 (loop B), Glu155 (loop B) and Tyr 97 (loop A) and a cation-π interaction with Tyr205, while the carboxylate group forms possible hydrogen bonds with Thr129 (β6 strand) and Thr202 (loop C) and a salt bridge with Arg66 (β2 strand).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model of GABA bound to the receptor, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The carboxylate group of GABA forms possible hydrogen bonds with Thr129 and Thr202.
source: The amino group of GABA likely forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Tyr157 (loop B), Glu155 (loop B) and Tyr 97 (loop A) and a cation-π interaction with Tyr205, while the carboxylate group forms possible hydrogen bonds with Thr129 (β6 strand) and Thr202 (loop C) and a salt bridge with Arg66 (β2 strand).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model of GABA bound to the receptor, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The carboxylate group of GABA forms a salt bridge with Arg66.
source: The amino group of GABA likely forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Tyr157 (loop B), Glu155 (loop B) and Tyr 97 (loop A) and a cation-π interaction with Tyr205, while the carboxylate group forms possible hydrogen bonds with Thr129 (β6 strand) and Thr202 (loop C) and a salt bridge with Arg66 (β2 strand).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model of GABA bound to the receptor, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tyr97, Glu155 and Arg66 are unique in the β subunit compared to the corresponding residues in the α and γ subunits and are crucial for substrate binding.
source: Notably, Tyr97, Glu155 and Arg66 are unique in the β subunit compared to the corresponding residues in the α and γ subunits and are crucial for substrate binding, as reported in previous studies demonstrating that Tyr97 and Arg66 play an important role in the binding pocket (Newell et al., 2004; Sander et al., 2011; Smith and Olsen, 1995).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure with previous functional studies (Newell et al., 2004; Sander et al., 2011; Smith and Olsen, 1995).

claim: Mutation of Tyr157 significantly reduces the binding affinity for agonist and antagonist.
source: Mutation of Tyr157, a highly conserved residue in the α, β and γ subunits, significantly reduces the binding affinity for agonist and antagonist (Lummis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Lummis, 2009).

claim: There is a well-defined glycosylation site at Asn110 of the α subunit, within the extracellular vestibule of the receptor.
source: There is a well-defined glycosylation site at Asn110 of the α subunit, within the extracellular vestibule of the receptor, at a site of post-translational modification that is distinct from the other GABAA receptor subunits (Figure 4A) and not observed before in any Cys-loop receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The glycosylation site at Asn110 of the α subunit is distinct from the other GABAA receptor subunits and not observed before in any Cys-loop receptor.
source: There is a well-defined glycosylation site at Asn110 of the α subunit, within the extracellular vestibule of the receptor, at a site of post-translational modification that is distinct from the other GABAA receptor subunits (Figure 4A) and not observed before in any Cys-loop receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with other GABAA receptor subunits and other Cys-loop receptor structures, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the α subunit at Asn110, a carbohydrate chain with seven sugar residues was built.
source: For the α subunit at Asn110 we have built a carbohydrate chain with seven sugar residues and, for the α* subunit at Asn 110, we have built a carbohydrate chain with four sugar groups (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is based on fitting the cryo-EM density with carbohydrate structures, as shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: For the α* subunit at Asn 110, a carbohydrate chain with four sugar groups was built.
source: For the α subunit at Asn110 we have built a carbohydrate chain with seven sugar residues and, for the α* subunit at Asn 110, we have built a carbohydrate chain with four sugar groups (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is based on fitting the cryo-EM density with carbohydrate structures, as shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The two carbohydrate chains at Asn110 are remarkably well ordered.
source: These two carbohydrate chains are remarkably well ordered, a feature that is likely due to the fact that the chains are contained within the extracellular vestibule and are in direct contact with numerous protein side chains (Figures 4A and 5).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density maps and inferred to be due to the structural constraints, as shown in Figures 4A and 5.

claim: The volume of glycosylation in the vestibule is approximately 700 Å3 at the contour level of 6 σ, which occupies nearly 18% of the total volume of the ECD vestibule.
source: The volume of glycosylation in the vestibule is approximately 700 Å3 at the contour level of 6 σ, which occupies nearly 18% of the total volume of the ECD vestibule.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: There are extensive and specific interactions observed between the sugar groups and the γ2S subunit involving residues Asn101, Lys112 and Trp123.
source: There are extensive and specific interactions observed between the sugar groups and the γ2S subunit involving residues Asn101, Lys112 and Trp123 (Figures 4A and 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figures 4A and 5.

claim: The glycosylation at Asn110 of the α subunits is important for subunit assembly, effectively blocking the formation of pentamers with more than two α subunits.
source: We propose that the glycosylation at Asn110 of the α subunits is important for subunit assembly, effectively blocking the formation of pentamers with more than two α subunits, due to the fact that more than two carbohydrate chains would engage in sterically prohibitive van der Waals clashes.
evidence: This is a proposal based on structural analysis and inference about steric constraints, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The contacts between the carbohydrate at position Asn110 of the α subunit and Trp123 of the γ2S subunit favor the inclusion of the γ subunit as the last subunit in the formation of the heteropentamer.
source: Moreover, we speculate that the contacts between the carbohydrate at position Asn110 of the α subunit and, for example, the Trp123 of the γ2S subunit, favor the inclusion of the γsubunit as the last subunit in the formation of the heteropentamer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed interactions in the structure.

claim: Glycosylation of the α subunit is essential for proper receptor assembly in mammalian cells.
source: This is consistent with prior studies which showed that glycosylation of the α subunit is essential for proper receptor assembly in mammalian cells (Buller et al., 1994), as well as the important role of tryptophan residues in interacting with carbohydrates in general (Maenaka et al., 1994; Stewart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Buller et al., 1994).

claim: Tryptophan residues play an important role in interacting with carbohydrates.
source: This is consistent with prior studies which showed that glycosylation of the α subunit is essential for proper receptor assembly in mammalian cells (Buller et al., 1994), as well as the important role of tryptophan residues in interacting with carbohydrates in general (Maenaka et al., 1994; Stewart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Maenaka et al., 1994; Stewart et al., 2008).

claim: The carbohydrate chains within the extracellular vestibule may modulate receptor gating and ion channel block by large ion channel blockers.
source: We further suggest that these carbohydrate chains within the extracellular vestibule may also modulate receptor gating and, perhaps, ion channel block by large ion channel blockers.
evidence: This is speculation based on the location and size of the glycosylation within the vestibule.

claim: The distances between the center of mass of two adjacent subunits in the TMD are similar, varying from 17.6 Å to 19 Å.
source: While the distances between the center of mass (COM) of two adjacent subunits are similar, where the COMs were calculated using the M1, M2 and M3 helices of each subunit, varying from 17.6 Å to 19 Å, the angles in the pentagon range from 94° to 124° (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The angles in the pentagon formed by the centers of mass of the TMD subunits range from 94° to 124°.
source: While the distances between the center of mass (COM) of two adjacent subunits are similar, where the COMs were calculated using the M1, M2 and M3 helices of each subunit, varying from 17.6 Å to 19 Å, the angles in the pentagon range from 94° to 124° (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two α M2 helices are located away from the other three TM helices.
source: Looking at the top-down views of five central M2 helices, the two α M2 helices are located away from the other three TM helices.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The M2 helices lining the pore in the β subunit display a similar orientation as in the desensitized state of the human β3 GABAA receptor.
source: The asymmetry in the TMD complicates defining whether the structure represents an open or closed state, as the M2 helices lining the pore in the β subunit display a similar orientation as in the desensitized state of the human β3 GABAA receptor, yet the α subunits are farther from the pseudo 5-fold axis, enlarging the pore (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure with the human β3 GABAA receptor structure, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The α subunits are farther from the pseudo 5-fold axis, enlarging the pore.
source: The asymmetry in the TMD complicates defining whether the structure represents an open or closed state, as the M2 helices lining the pore in the β subunit display a similar orientation as in the desensitized state of the human β3 GABAA receptor, yet the α subunits are farther from the pseudo 5-fold axis, enlarging the pore (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The TMD structure may represent a non-native conformation due to the asymmetric structure and the fact that the structure was solved using a receptor embedded in a detergent micelle.
source: Because of the asymmetric structure of the TMD and the fact that the structure was solved using a receptor embedded in a detergent micelle, the TMD structure may represent a non-native conformation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed asymmetry and the use of detergent micelles.

claim: The larger contact areas in the ECD region make formation of the β(+)/α(-) interface favorable, leading to α/β assembly intermediates.
source: If we consider how heteromeric GABAA receptors form from α, β and γ subunits, we speculate that the larger contact areas in the ECD region makes formation of the β(+)/α(-) interface favorable, thus leading to α/β assembly intermediates, which then transition to (α/β)2 intermediates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the buried surface area analysis reported in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The glycosylation at Asn110 of the α subunits disfavors addition of a third α subunit due to steric clashes.
source: The crucial glycosylation site on the α subunit at Asn110 disfavors addition of a third α subunit, due to steric clashes, and that either a β or a γ subunit will be incorporated to complete the heteropentamer (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Either a β or a γ subunit will be incorporated to complete the heteropentamer after formation of (α/β)2 intermediates.
source: The crucial glycosylation site on the α subunit at Asn110 disfavors addition of a third α subunit, due to steric clashes, and that either a β or a γ subunit will be incorporated to complete the heteropentamer (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The glycosylation at Asn110 of the α subunits may be important to ion channel function.
source: Thus, the glycosylation at Asn110 of the α subunits not only plays an important role in ion channel assembly, but it may also be important to ion channel function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the location of the glycosylation within the extracellular vestibule.

claim: Diazepam binds to the α*(+)/γ(-) interface with high affinity.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that diazepam binds to the α*(+)/γ(-) interface with high affinity (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Li et al., 2013).

claim: α*His101 could provide aromatic or hydrophobic interactions with the pendant phenyl ring of diazepam.
source: In agreement with previous studies, we speculate that α*His101 could provide aromatic or hydrophobic interactions with the pendant phenyl ring of diazepam.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model and comparison with previous studies.

claim: α*Tyr209, α*Phe99, α*Tyr159 and γPhe77 likely contribute to hydrophobic interactions with diazepam.
source: Additionally, α*Tyr209, α*Phe99, α*Tyr159 and γPhe77 likely also contribute to hydrophobic interactions with diazepam (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model shown in Figure 3F.

claim: All key structural residues surrounding the diazepam site have been identified in homology models and functional experiments.
source: All these key structural residues surrounding the diazepam site have been identified in homology models and functional experiments (Richter et al., 2012; Teissére and Czajkowski, 2001; Wongsamitkul et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Richter et al., 2012; Teissére and Czajkowski, 2001; Wongsamitkul et al., 2017).

claim: Mutation of α*His101, α*Tyr209 and α*Tyr159 markedly impairs the modulation by diazepam.
source: Indeed, mutation of α*His101, α*Tyr209 and α*Tyr159 markedly impairs the modulation by diazepam (Amin et al., 1997), while mutation of γPhe77 results in decreased binding affinity.
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Amin et al., 1997).

claim: Mutation of γPhe77 results in decreased binding affinity for diazepam.
source: Indeed, mutation of α*His101, α*Tyr209 and α*Tyr159 markedly impairs the modulation by diazepam (Amin et al., 1997), while mutation of γPhe77 results in decreased binding affinity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though no specific citation is provided for the γPhe77 mutation effect.

claim: Agonist binding has been proposed to induce loop C closure in the open, ion conducting state.
source: Agonist binding has been proposed to induce loop C closure in the open, ion conducting state and antagonist binding to stabilize an 'open' configuration of loop C in the closed, non-conducting state of the ion channel (Du et al., 2015; Mukhtasimova et al., 2005; Purohit and Auerbach, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Du et al., 2015; Mukhtasimova et al., 2005; Purohit and Auerbach, 2013).

claim: Antagonist binding stabilizes an 'open' configuration of loop C in the closed, non-conducting state of the ion channel.
source: Agonist binding has been proposed to induce loop C closure in the open, ion conducting state and antagonist binding to stabilize an 'open' configuration of loop C in the closed, non-conducting state of the ion channel (Du et al., 2015; Mukhtasimova et al., 2005; Purohit and Auerbach, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Du et al., 2015; Mukhtasimova et al., 2005; Purohit and Auerbach, 2013).

claim: Loop C in the β* subunit is in an 'open' conformation relative to that in the α* and γ subunits.
source: To probe the relationship between agonist binding and the position of loop C, we superposed the β* subunit with GABA bound onto the α* and γ subunits and found that loop C in the β* subunit is in an 'open' conformation relative to that in the α* and γ subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The position of loop C in the β* subunit closely approximates that in the GlyR-closed non-conducting state.
source: Additionally, superposition of the ECD of the β*/α subunit with the human β3 GABAA, GlyR-open and GlyR-closed structures suggests that the position of loop C in the β* subunit closely approximates that in the GlyR-closed non-conducting state, while loop C in the human β3 GABAA is in a more 'open' configuration (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Loop C in the human β3 GABAA is in a more 'open' configuration compared to the β* subunit in the α1β1γ2SEM structure.
source: Additionally, superposition of the ECD of the β*/α subunit with the human β3 GABAA, GlyR-open and GlyR-closed structures suggests that the position of loop C in the β* subunit closely approximates that in the GlyR-closed non-conducting state, while loop C in the human β3 GABAA is in a more 'open' configuration (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor was expressed in TSA201 suspension cells using baculovirus transduction.
source: The tri-heteromer (α1β1γ2SEM) was expressed in TSA201 suspension cells. Infection was performed at a cell density of 1.5−3 × 106 cells/mL in Gibco Freestyle 293 Expression medium supplemented with 1% FBS and placed in a humidity- and CO2-controlled incubator.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The α1β1γ2SEM receptor was purified using 1D4 affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography.
source: The supernatant was then mixed with 1D4 affinity resin equilibrated in 20 mM NaPO4 pH 8, 200 mM NaCl, and 1 mM C12M for 3–4 hr at 4°C with gentle mixing. The resin was washed with 100 column volumes of the equilibration buffer; elution was achieved using a buffer supplemented with 0.2 mM 1D4 peptide. The eluted protein was concentrated by ultrafiltration, followed by the addition of 2.1 molar fold excess of 8E3 Fab. The concentrated sample was loaded onto a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column equilibrated with 20 mM HEPES pH 7.3, 200 mM NaCl, 1 mM C12M and 1.5 mM GABA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The cryo-EM structure was determined using graphene oxide coated grids.
source: To enhance particle density on the cryo-EM grids in light of modest levels of receptor expression, we employed grids coated with graphene oxide.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: A total of 1391 movie stacks were collected for cryo-EM data analysis.
source: A total of 1391 movie stacks were collected and correction for beam-induced motion was carried out using MotionCor2 (Zheng et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: 1097 'good' micrographs were retained for image analysis after initial screening.
source: Micrographs with large areas of ice contamination, multiple layers of graphene oxide, defocus values larger than −2.5 μm or defocus values smaller than −1.2 μm were deleted. Thus 1097 'good' micrographs were retained for the following image analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methods.

claim: There is substantial preferred orientation in the particle distribution.
source: We note that there is substantial preferred orientation in the particle distribution and, despite substantial efforts in exploring a wide spectrum of conditions, we were unable to obtain grids that yielded more well distributed particle orientations.
evidence: This is an observation about the quality of the cryo-EM data, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The density for the TMD is not as well defined as the density in the ECD.
source: Inspection of the resulting density maps were consistent with these resolution estimations, and in the case of the density in the extracellular domain (ECD), the quality of the density map is excellent, allowing for visualization of medium and large side chains, as well as glycosylation of Asn side chains (Figure 1—figure supplement 6). By contrast, the density for the TMD is not as well defined.
evidence: This is an observation about the quality of the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The M4 helices of the two α1 subunits and the γ2S subunit have weak density and were not included in the structure.
source: While the M1, M2 and M3 helices of all subunits show strong density, with density for some residues with large side chains, the M4 helices of the two α1 subunits and the γ2S subunit have weak density and thus we have not attempted to include them in the structure.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of the structural model due to weak density.

claim: The EC50 for GABA is 28.68 μM in the absence of Fab.
source: EC50 = 28.68 μM (95% CI = 21.38–38.49 μM) or 22.51 μM (95% CI = 12.69–39.93 μM) GABA in the presence or absence of 25 nM Fab, respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: The EC50 for GABA is 22.51 μM in the presence of 25 nM Fab.
source: EC50 = 28.68 μM (95% CI = 21.38–38.49 μM) or 22.51 μM (95% CI = 12.69–39.93 μM) GABA in the presence or absence of 25 nM Fab, respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: The 8E3 antibody is specific for the α1 subunit.
source: Subsequent FSEC analysis identified 8E3 as a α1 specific antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The map correlation coefficient between the ECD model and the ECD map is 0.80.
source: After phenix refinement, the map correlation coefficient (CC) between the map and the ECD model was 0.80, indicative of a good fit between the ECD model and the ECD map.
evidence: This is a measure of the quality of the structural model fit to the cryo-EM density.

claim: The map correlation coefficient between the whole model and the whole map is 0.74.
source: After phenix refinement, the CC between the whole map model and whole map was 0.74.
evidence: This is a measure of the quality of the structural model fit to the cryo-EM density.
